4.1.4.Reranking Experiments
We evaluated the impact of the BGE reranker by comparing performance across all ICL variations both with and without the reranking component. For the reranking experiments, we (i) retrieved an initial set of 20 candidate documents using BM25, (ii) applied the BGE cross-encodertorerankthesecandidates, and(iii)selectedthetop-5documentsafterreranking for rationale generation. We chose 20 initial candidates and kept the top-5 after reranking as an empirically validated, budget-awaresettingthatmatchescommontwo-stageretrievalpracticeandpreserved our token/latency constraints.
4.1.5.Retrieval Method
For document retrieval, we initially used the MedCPT retriever. However, to simplify our experimental pipeline and conserve computational resources, we transitioned to BM25. ThischangewassupportedbysimilarperformancemetricsbetweenBM25andmorecomplex retrievers in our preliminary evaluations.
4.1.6.Model
For all experiments, we used Llama-3-8B-Instruct for both reasoning generation (in the case of InstructRAG-ICL) and answer generation (for both InstructRAG-ICL and Vanilla RAG) (see subsection 4.1.1)
4.2.Human Evaluation Setup
To assess the quality of generated rationales and validate our automatic evaluation metrics, we designed a human annotation study with the following components:
4.2.1.Annotation Protocol
Two annotators with extensive experience in NLP systems independently evaluated a conveniencesampleof4examples(2perdataset). Whilethissamplesizeprecludesstatistical inference, it allowed us to (i) validate the clarity of our 8-category taxonomy, (ii) identify systematic differences between human and LLM judgments, and (iii) surface failure modes for qualitative analysis. For each example, annotators evaluated: •Overall Response Quality: A 1-5 scale rating the comprehensiveness and correctness of the final answer. •Rationale-Context Alignment: Classifying each reasoning statement according to its faithfulness to the retrieved documents using eight predefined categories. •Faithfulness Score: A numeric score on how much the response is grounded in the provided context.
4.2.2.LLM-as-a-Judge Implementation
In parallel with human annotation, we implemented an automated evaluation using a large language model (GPT-4o) to assess the system output on the same examples used for the human evaluation. The automated judge was provided with: (i) the original question, (ii)retrievedcontextdocuments, (iii)thegeneratedrationale, and(iv)thegeneratedanswer. The LLM judge was instructed to evaluate using the same criteria as human annotators.

title: Reason and Verify: A Framework for Faithful Retrieval-Augmented Generation
text:
5.Results
We present our experimental findings in three parts: (1) comparison with published baselines, (2) ablation analysis of our framework components, and (3) analysis of demonstration selection strategies.
5.1.Comparison with Baselines
[TABLE: compares our configurations against published MIRAGE baselines. Despite using]
Llama-3-8B-Instruct—a model roughly 10×smaller than GPT-4—our framework achieves competitive or superior performance. On BioASQ-Y/N, our best configuration (3-shot Dynamic ICL with reranking) achieves 89.1% accuracy, approaching MedRAG+GPT-3.5 (90.29%). On PubMedQA*, our 0-shot rationale generation achieves73.0%, exceeding MedRAG+GPT-4 (70.60%) by 2.4 points absolute. We attribute this to explicit rationale generation: by requiring the model to articulate evidence-linked reasoning before answering, we reduce hallucinated inferences that may arise in larger models operating without such structure. Notably, while MedRAG uses a four-corpus ensemble (MedCorp) with reciprocal rank fusion over four retrievers (RRF-4), our system uses only PubMed with BM25 + BGE reranking—a substantially simpler retrieval pipeline. This suggests that reasoning-side improvements (rationale generation, dynamic ICL) can compensate for retrieval complexity.
5.2.Ablation Study
[TABLE: isolates the contribution of each framework component. We report results across]
different numbers of in-context demonstrations to understand interactions between components.
5.2.1.Effect of Reranking
Reranking with the BGE cross-encoder provides consistent benefits, particularly for Pub- MedQA in few-shot settings. The most dramatic improvement occurs in the 4-shot Pub- MedQA setting, where reranking improves accuracy from 47.5% to 60.0% (+12.5 points). This suggests that reranking helps filter out noisy passages that would otherwise mislead the model when combined with multiple demonstrations. For BioASQ, reranking yields modest but consistent gains in the 0–2 shot range (+0.9 to +1.6 points). The slight degradation at 3-shot (-1.3 points) may indicate that high-quality demonstrations can partially compensate for retrieval noise.
5.2.2.Effect of Dynamic Demonstration Selection
Dynamic ICL selection via KNN retrieval substantially outperforms static demonstration selection across all few-shot configurations. The improvements are particularly pronounced for BioASQ, where dynamic selection at 4-shot yields +14.5 points over static selection (86.2% vs. 71.7%). Notably, dynamic selection reverses the degradation pattern observed with static ICL. Under static selection, adding more demonstrationshurtsperformance on both datasets (BioASQ drops from 85.8% at 0-shot to 70.4% at 4-shot). With dynamic selection, performance remains stable or improves, peaking at 3-shot for BioASQ (89.1%) and 2-shot for PubMedQA (71.0%).

title: Reason and Verify: A Framework for Faithful Retrieval-Augmented Generation
text:
5.3.Analysis of Demonstration Sensitivity
PubMedQA exhibits higher sensitivity to demonstration selection than BioASQ. We attribute this to two factors: (i) the ternary classification structure (yes/no/maybe) creates label-prior bias when demonstrations are not carefully balanced, and (ii) PubMed abstracts arelonger, causingadditionaldemonstrationstocompetewithretrievedevidenceforcontext window space.
6.Limitations
Despite promising results on biomedical question answering, our study has several limitations. First, evaluation is limited to two English biomedical datasets (BioASQ and Pub- MedQA), which may reduce generalizability to other domains, languages, or question formats. Both benchmarks largely emphasize factoid and binary judgments; performance on more complex settings (e.g., multi-hop or causal reasoning) remains untested. Second, parts of our pipeline rely on OpenAI API calls, introducing additional latency and monetary cost that may hinder deployment at scale. Exploring open-source substitutes for these components is an important direction for future work. Third, we do not evaluate in real clinical workflows or with clinicians in the loop. Our system is intended as a research prototype for studying rationale generation and verification rather than a clinical decision support tool. Any high-stakes deployment would require substantially more validation and safety measures. Fourth, we report single-point accuracy estimates without statistical significance testing or confidence intervals. While our ablation design isolates component contributions, the magnitude of improvements should be interpreted with appropriate caution until replicated across multiple runs. Finally, our human evaluation is small (4 examples annotated by 2 raters). Larger studies are needed to reliably assess rationale quality, agreement, and the practical utility of explicit reasoning for biomedical QA.
7.Demo
A functional demonstration of the proposed system is available on HuggingFace1. In this interactive application, users can query an AI-related white paper, and the system responds with both a generated answer and a transparent rationale. Specifically, the interface displays the supporting evidence passages retrieved from the document collection and explains how they were integrated into the model’s response. This allows users to assess the relevance of the retrieved information and the robustness of the underlying retrieval-augmented generation pipeline.
AppendixA.Pilot Human Study: Per-Example Faithfulness Scores
As an illustrative complement to our pilot human evaluation (4 examples total), Table 4 reports the per-example faithfulness scoresFaith(R)(Eq. 3.1) assigned by two human annotators and the LLM verifier. We include these values to qualitatively examine agreement patterns and to illustrate cases where the automated verifier appears more strict or more permissive than the human raters. Given the small sample size, these results are descriptive and should not be interpreted as statistically reliable estimates of verifier performance. The LLM verifier tends to assign higher faithfulness scores than human annotators (mean 0.94 vs. 0.85 and 0.65), suggesting it may be more permissive in accepting implicit reasoning. B.2.1.PubMedQA Prompt

OUTPUT FORMAT REQUIREMENT:End your response with exactly one of the following on a new line: “FINAL ANSWER: A. yes” “FINAL ANSWER: B. no” “FINAL ANSWER: C. maybe” If no document supports an answer, output: “ANSWER UNAVAILABLE”
B.2.2.BioASQ Prompt
BioASQ requires binary classification (yes/no). We appended: Provide a precise factual answer grounded in the documents. Extract relevant statements and justify the decision based strictly on presented facts. title: RetrievalQA: Assessing Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Short-form Open-Domain Question Answering
text:
RetrievalQA: Assessing Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Short-form Open-Domain Question Answering Zihan Zhang1, Meng Fang2, Ling Chen1
1University of Technology Sydney2University of Liverpool
Zihan.Zhang-5@student.uts.edu.au ,Meng.Fang@liverpool.ac.uk Ling.Chen@uts.edu.au
Abstract
Adaptive retrieval-augmented generation (ARAG) aims to dynamically determine the necessity of retrieval for queries instead of retrieving indiscriminately to enhance the efficiency and relevance of the sourced information. However, previous works largely overlook the evaluation of ARAG approaches, leading to their effectiveness being understudied. This work presents a benchmark, RetrievalQA , comprising 1,271 short-form questions covering new world and long-tail knowledge. The knowledge necessary to answer the questions is absent from LLMs; therefore, external information must be retrieved to answer correctly. This makes RetrievalQA a suitable testbed to evaluate existing ARAG methods. We observe that calibration-based methods heavily rely on threshold tuning, while vanilla prompting is inadequate for guiding LLMs to make reliable retrieval decisions. Based on our findings, we propose Time-Aware Adaptive REtrieval (TA-ARE ), a simple yet effective method that helps LLMs assess the necessity of retrieval without calibration or additional training1.
1 Introduction
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) (Guu et al., 2020; Lewis et al., 2020; Ram et al., 2023) that augments large language models (LLMs) with retrieval of relevant information has become increasingly popular in knowledge-intensive tasks, including open-domain question-answering (QA) (Zhang et al., 2023b; Kasai et al., 2023; Cui et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023a). However, standard RAG methods conduct retrieval indiscriminately , irrespective of the input query, which may result in suboptimal task performance and increased inference costs (Gao et al., 2024). We find that Self-RAG requires threshold tuning to balance QA performance and retrieval efficiency, while vanilla prompting is insufficient in guiding LLMs to make reliable retrieval decisions (§3.3). Below : an error analysis for GPT-3.5. At least half of the time, GPT-3.5 is unaware that it needs retrieval ( i.e.,Red area, §3.4). encode vast knowledge in parameters through largescale pre-training, enabling them to effortlessly handle straightforward queries without retrieval (Mallen et al., 2023). On the other hand, the retrieved context may contain noise and irrelevant information, and augmenting noisy context can potentially distract LLMs, thereby impeding task performance (Shi et al., 2023). To alleviate the limitations of RAG mentioned above, recent studies advocate for adaptive RAG (ARAG) , which dynamically determines retrieval necessity and relies only on LLMs’ parametric knowledge when deemed unnecessary (Feng et al.,

title: RetrievalQA: Assessing Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Short-form Open-Domain Question Answering
text:
ods is understudied, as there is no suitable benchmark and evaluation. ARAG approaches can be categorized into calibration-based andmodel-based judgement. Calibration-based methods (Mallen et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2023; Asai et al., 2023b), while effective, trigger retrieval only when a metric surpasses a pre-defined threshold. For example, Mallen et al. (2023) heuristically retrieve when the popularity of an entity on Wikipedia is below a certain threshold; Jiang et al. (2023) trigger retrieval if any token in the temporarily generated sentence has low confidence. Clearly, these ad-hoc calibrationbased methods are suboptimal, as we need to tune thresholds for different datasets and models to balance task performance and inference overheads. To obviate the hyperparameter threshold, model-based methods (Feng et al., 2023a; Ren et al., 2023) directly prompt LLMs for retrieval decisions, given the observation that LLMs can acknowledge their knowledge boundaries to some extent (Kadavath et al., 2022; Yin et al., 2023). These methods undergo separate evaluations, and their effectiveness remains ambiguous due to the limited scope of the assessments. In this paper, we investigate to what extent LLMs can perform calibration-free adaptive retrieval via prompting. To answer this question, we need to evaluate whether LLMs retrieve only when necessary. This requests a benchmark that distinguishes between questions that can be answered using LLMs’ parametric knowledge and those that require external information through retrieval. Nevertheless, commonly used open-domain QA datasets (Rajpurkar et al., 2016; Joshi et al., 2017; Kwiatkowski et al., 2019; Mallen et al., 2023) fail to fulfil this purpose, as various LLMs have distinct sizes and levels of pre-trained knowledge, making them inadequately assess the necessity of external retrieval for LLMs. To fill this gap, we create RetrievalQA , a shortform QA dataset, covering new world and long-tail knowledge and spanning diverse topics. We ensure the knowledge necessary to answer the questions is absent from LLMs. Therefore, LLMs must truthfully decide whether to retrieve to be able to answer the questions correctly. RetrievalQA enables us to evaluate the effectiveness of ARAG approaches, an aspect predominantly overlooked in prior studies and recent RAG evaluation systems (Chen et al., 2023; Saad-Falcon et al., 2023; Es et al., 2023), which focus only on task performance, the relevance of retrieval context or the faithfulness of an-swers. Using RetrievalQA as a testbed, we benchmark both calibration-based and model-based methods with varying sizes of LLMs. As shown in Fig.1, we find calibration-based Self-RAG requires threshold tuning to balance QA performance and retrieval efficiency, while vanilla prompting is insufficient in guiding LLMs to make reliable retrieval decisions. As an initial effort, we propose Time-Aware Adaptive REtrieval ( TA-ARE ), a simple yet effective method to improve ARAG via in-context learning (ICL; Brown et al. 2020), obviating the need for calibration or additional training. To sum up, this paper makes the following contributions: 1we create a new dataset RetrievalQA to assess ARAG for short-form open-domain QA; 2we benchmark existing methods and conduct extensive analysis, finding that vanilla prompting is insufficient in guiding LLMs to make reliable retrieval decisions; 3we then propose TA-ARE, a simple yet effective method to help LLMs assess the necessity of retrieval without calibration or additional training.
2 Dataset Construction
Data collection. Inspired by Zhuang et al. (2023), we aim to collect data such that the knowledge necessary to answer the questions is absent from LLMs. Therefore, LLMs must consult external resources to answer correctly. Specifically, we mainly collect data from two categories: 1New world knowledge that is out of the scope of the LLMs’ pretraining corpora. LLMs are static after training and can quickly be outdated due to the ever-changing world (Zhang et al., 2023b). To ensure the knowledge is novel to most LLMs, we select 397 QA pairs ranging from 1 October 2023 to 12 January 2024 from RealTimeQA (Kasai et al., 2023). These data comprise weekly quizzes extracted from news websites, encompassing broad topics, including politics, business, and entertainment. In addition, we collect 127 fast-changing questions from FreshQA (Vu et al., 2023), where the answers may change frequently, thereby challenging LLMs’ parametric memorization. 2Long-tail knowledge that is rarely learned during pre-training. Previous studies (Kandpal et al., 2023) have shown that LLMs struggle to learn less common knowledge and perform poorly without the help of retrieval. Following Asai et al. (2023b), we use the longtail subset of PopQA (Mallen et al., 2023), which

3RetrievalQA Challenges Adaptive RAG
In this section, we formalize ARAG for opendomain QA tasks and evaluate existing adaptive approaches on RetrievalQA .
3.1 Standard & Adaptive RAG for QA
Standard RAG. Given a question x, a retriever R, and an external document corpus Dsuch as Wikipedia, the retriever first retrieves a list of rele-

on a prompt instruction I, retrieved documents Dx, and the question x. Adaptive RAG. Standard RAG always retrieves regardless of the input question, while adaptive re-trieval only retrieves when necessary. Calibrationbased methods generally introduce a pre-defined hyperparameter tand only do retrieval when a metric surpasses t: y=LLM(I,Dx, x),metric ≥t LLM(I, x), otherwise Baselines. While our primary focus is model-based methods, we also evaluate the most recent state-ofthe-art Self-RAG (7B) (Asai et al., 2023b). Self- RAG fine-tunes Llama-2 using special reflection tokens to allow the model to introspect its outputs. The model activates retrieval when the probabilities of the generated special tokens exceed a threshold. ForModel-based methods, we follow Feng et al. (2023a) and Ren et al. (2023) to instruct LLMs to decide whether to retrieve via prompting, obviating the threshold. Specifically, we ask a yes/no question:r=LLM(Ivanilla, x), where Ivanilla ="Given a question, determine whether you need to retrieve ... answer [Yes] or [No]" .Retrieval is performed only when LLMs answer yes. We denote this as Vanilla prompting: y=LLM(I,Dx, x), r=Yes LLM(I, x), otherwise Baselines. We evaluate strong instruction-tuned models with a varying scale of model size: TinyLlama (1.1B; Zhang et al. 2024), Phi-2 (2.7B; Li et al. 2023), Llama-2 (7B; Touvron et al. 2023), GPT-3.5 (OpenAI, 2022), and GPT-4 (OpenAI, 2023).
3.2 Experiment Setup
Evaluation Metric. We use retrieval accuracy to evaluate how well LLMs can perform adaptive retrieval. Since all questions in our dataset need retrieval, the higher the retrieval accuracy, the more effective the method. Following Schick et al. (2023); Mallen et al. (2023); Asai et al. 4.1 Method
Based on our findings in §3.4, we propose Time- Aware Adaptive REtrieval via ICL ( TA-ARE ), a simple yet effective method to improve ARAG without calibration or additional training. Given that new world knowledge questions often contain time-sensitive information ( e.g., "last week", "recent"), we include "Today is current_date() "in the instruction to enhance models’ awareness of time. For long-tail knowledge, we use SimCSE (Gao et al., 2021) to select top-2 semantically closest long-tail questions answered incorrectly from the discarded set in §2, denoted as [Yes] demonstrations. For [No] demonstrations, we manually create another two questions, ensuring no extra information is required for most LLMs to answer (e.g.,What is the capital of France? ). Time Example Avg. 5 Conclusion
This paper presents a new dataset RetrievalQA to assess adaptive RAG for short-form open-domain QA. We find vanilla prompting is insufficient in guiding LLMs to make reliable retrieval decisions. As an initial attempt, we propose TA-ARE, a simple yet effective method to help LLMs assess the necessity of retrieval, obviating the need for calibration or additional training.

title: RetrievalQA: Assessing Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Short-form Open-Domain Question Answering
text:
Limitations We identify the limitations of our work as follows: •We mainly collect data from existing data sources and use GPT-4 for filtering out answerable questions. While we have done preliminary human checking in Appendix A.5, it is possible that some questions in the dataset do not require additional information for LLMs to answer. Future work could develop advanced algorithms to do more efficient and rigour filtering. •We primarily focus on short-form QA in this paper and do not assess long-form generation tasks. It should be noted that methods, including Jiang et al. (2023); Asai et al. (2023b), are capable of long-form generation tasks. Self-RAG can also perform sophisticated selfreflection, which goes beyond adaptive retrieval. •We acknowledge that some of the retrieved documents may not contain the answers or the information needed to answer the questions. While improving retrieval relevance and accuracy is out of the scope of this paper, noisy context may interfere with LLMs and hurt the QA performance. •While we find our prompt templates work well, we do not perform prompt tuning in this paper. We acknowledge that prompt templates can be sensitive to LLMs, and there are methods to find optimal prompts (Shin et al., 2020; Deng et al., 2022). We believe optimal prompts can be found and further improve performance. We leave this as a future work. Ethical Statement TheRetrievalQA dataset, meticulously curated to evaluate LLMs’ self-awareness ability to decide when to retrieve external resources, is constructed only using publicly available data sources. We rigorously vetted the licenses of the five publicly available datasets for compliance, ensuring that all our research methodologies aligned with institutional, national, and global ethical standards. We carefully examine the data to ensure no privacy concerns or violations. We do not collect any personally identifiable information. All data used in this paper is obtained following legal and ethicalstandards. In addition, we adhere to the terms of use and policies of OpenAI and Meta. text:
RealTimeQA (Kasai et al., 2023) A dynamic question-answering (QA) based on weeklypublished news articles, which challenges static LLMs. We select data from 1 October 2023 to 12 January 2024. These data comprise weekly quizzes extracted from news websites, encompassing broad topics, including politics, business, and entertainment. FreshQA (Vu et al., 2023) A QA benchmark with 600 questions that cover a wide range of questions and answer types. We use the fast-changing subset so that the knowledge memorized in LLMs can potentially be outdated, thus requiring external new information. ToolQA (Zhuang et al., 2023) A benchmark to faithfully evaluate LLMs’ ability to use external tools. We use questions from the Personal Agenda domain, which consists of 100 synthesized questions with virtual names and events. PopQA (Mallen et al., 2023) An entity-centric open-domain QA dataset about entities with a wide variety of popularity. We use the long-tail subset of the data. TriviaQA (Joshi et al., 2017) A reading comprehension dataset containing question-answerevidence triples. We follow Asai et al. (2023b) and use the test split of the unfiltered version.
A.2 Details of RetrievalQA Construction
In this section, we discuss the details of our dataset construction. Our goal is to evaluate adaptive RAG (ARAG) methods and see how good they are at deciding when to retrieve. Therefore, we need the ground truth labels for each question’s retrieval necessity. Ultimately, there are three kinds of questions here: •Case 1: for all LLMs, questions that can be answered using only their parametric knowledge •Case 2: for all LLMs, questions that can not be answered using only the parametric knowledge, therefore requiring external retrieval •Case 3: questions that can be answered with their parametric knowledge for some models but can not be answered for some other modelsWe do not consider Case 3 because those questions cannot fairly measure whether retrieval is required for different LLMs. For Case 1, it is not trivia to collect questions that can be answered only using the parametric knowledge of LLMs. This is because different LLMs have different levels of pre-trained knowledge, and it is hard to measure (Petroni et al., 2019; Kadavath et al., 2022). For example, given a question, GPT-3.5 may fail to answer and need the help of external knowledge, while Llama-2 may answer correctly using its own knowledge because it has seen the question in the training data. The pre-training corpora are sometimes unavailable, especially for proprietary models, and we can not guarantee that the collected questions can be 100% answered with their own knowledge, as shown in the table below. However, different from Cases 1 and 3, for Case 2, theoretically, it is possible to collect data that guarantees the knowledge to answer the questions is not present in the models. For instance, new world knowledge occurred after model training and long-tail knowledge that did not (or rarely) appear in the training corpora. Therefore, we collect 1,271 questions (Case 2) that are guaranteed cannot be answered without external information. The data collection process is detailed in §2. The dataset statistics are shown in Table 3. The examples of data instances are in Table 11. To avoid potential bias in the evaluation towards methods that retrieve more often, we additionally collect 1,514 questions (Case 1) that can be answered using GPT-2’s parametric knowledge from the discard set. Specifically, we use GPT-2 (small, 124M) in the zero-shot closed-book QA setting to evaluate the discard set. We only keep questions that can be answered using GPT-2’s paramet-

assuming that larger and stronger LLMs are also highly likely to succeed if small and weak GPT-2 can answer correctly without retrieval. We also use the entire PopQA dataset (the rest of the longtail split), which has 12,883 data instances that are more common on the web. We found that GPT-2 cannot answer any new-world questions from the discard set, which is reasonable.

title: TopoChunker: Topology-Aware Agentic Document Chunking Framework
text:
TopoChunker: Topology-Aware Agentic Document Chunking Framework Xiaoyu Liu Independent Researcher liushifu986938279@gmail.com
Abstract
Current document chunking methods for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) typically linearize text. This forced linearization strips away intrinsic topological hierarchies, creating “semantic fragmentation” that degrades downstream retrieval quality. In this paper, we propose TopoChunker, an agentic framework that maps heterogeneous documents onto a Structured Intermediate Representation (SIR) to explicitly preserve cross-segment dependencies. To balance structural fidelity with computational cost, TopoChunker employs a dual-agent architecture. An Inspector Agent dynamically routes documents through costoptimized extraction paths, while a Refiner Agent performs capacity auditing and topological context disambiguation to reconstruct hierarchical lineage. Evaluated on unstructured narratives (GutenQA) and complex reports (GovReport), TopoChunker demonstrates state-of-the-art performance. It outperforms the strongest LLM-based baseline by 8.0% in absolute generation accuracy and achieves an 83.26% Recall@3, while simultaneously reducing token overhead by 23.5%, offering a scalable approach for structure-aware RAG.
1 Introduction
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) mitigates Large Language Model (LLM) hallucinations by grounding generation in external knowledge. While long-context LLMs have continuously improved, fine-grained retrieval remains essential due to lower inference costs and the necessity to avoid the “Lost in the Middle” phenomenon. Consequently, document chunking acts as the foundational semantic filter in the RAG pipeline, directly determining the upper bound of downstream retrieval quality. However, conventional chunking tools rely on static heuristics that are agnostic to inherent document topology. Even emerging LLM-based chun-kers (e.g., LumberChunker) predominantly operate under a rigid “text-to-text” paradigm, flattening complex, multi-modal documents (such as enterprise PDFs) into linear text streams. This forced linearization introduces three main issues: visualsemantic disconnect, contextual fragmentation, and feature dilution. Such mechanical splitting strips chunks of their hierarchical topology, creating “semantic islands” that isolate context-dependent terminology and cause anaphoric ambiguity. Furthermore, fully generative chunkers apply computationally expensive LLM reasoning uniformly across all text, resulting in redundant token expenditures on structurally simple content. To address these structural and computational constraints, we propose TopoChunker, a topologyaware framework for structural-fidelity document chunking. Unlike linear pipelines, TopoChunker treats documents as heterogeneous entities and maps them onto a shared Structured Intermediate Representation (SIR). Driven by a collaborative dual-agent architecture—an Inspector Agent for routing and a Refiner Agent for semantic auditing—the system systematically bridges the gap between fragmented raw text and contextually self-contained RAG inputs. Our primary contributions are summarized as follows: •Adaptive Routing via Inspector Agent:We introduce a dynamic routing mechanism that actively probes document complexity. It optimizes the cost-fidelity trade-off by selectively applying rule-based slicing for standard layouts and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for complex visual structures, thereby avoiding uniform LLM overhead. •Topological Modeling & Atomicity-Aware Execution:We propose the Structured Intermediate Representation (SIR) protocol to de-

title: TopoChunker: Topology-Aware Agentic Document Chunking Framework
text:
soning. Combined with a stack-based traversal algorithm and Atomicity Locking, this inmemory graph preserves logical hierarchies and prevents the physical fragmentation of indivisible units (e.g., cross-page tables). •Context Disambiguation via Refiner Agent: We design a diagnostic Refiner Agent that autonomously resolves contextual voids, such as grounding dangling pronouns and deciphering isolated terminology, to generate selfcontained chunks. Extensive evaluations show that TopoChunker yields state-of-the-art performance, outperforming the strongest baseline by an absolute margin of 8.0% in endto-end generation accuracy and achieving 83.26% Recall@3, alongside a 23.5% reduction in token consumption.
2 Related Work
2.1 Granularity Evolution: From Heuristic
Rules to Semantic Sensitivity Document chunking strategies have advanced from rigid, fixed-length heuristics to flexible, semanticdriven approaches. Traditional fixed-size chunking serves as the baseline, partitioning text into segments of predefined character or token lengths, often employing an overlap window to mitigate boundary fragmentation. While simple to implement, this approach frequently leads to semantic misalignment in structured documents. Recursive character chunking improves upon this by using prioritized delimiters to split text until segments fall below a threshold, making it better suited for hierarchical content. To further align with semantic boundaries, semantic-aware techniques have emerged. Semantic Chunker (Xiao et al., 2024) utilizes embedding similarity thresholds to merge sentence-level units, enhancing intra-chunk coherence. However, its performance remains contingent on embedding quality, and it often struggles with long-tail distributions in complex documents. Meta-Chunking (Zhao et al., 2024) introduces model-derived signals like perplexity fluctuations, while Lumber- Chunker (Duarte et al., 2024) explicitly leverages LLM reasoning to define boundaries. Despite these advances, the “feature dilution” problem persists: oversized chunks cause embedding vectors to shift toward noisy centroids, reducing retrieval discriminability. Furthermore, these methods are largely confined to single-granularity paradigms, failingto capture multi-dimensional topological features. TopoChunker addresses these structural limitations through its Structured Intermediate Representation (SIR), enabling dynamic granularity adjustment and explicit topology awareness.
2.2 Hierarchical Representation and Context
Augmentation in RAG The efficacy of RAG systems is significantly influenced by the structured presentation of retrieved passages, as different queries necessitate varying levels of abstraction. AutoChunker (Jain et al., 2025) organizes information into tree structures but focuses primarily on static noise suppression rather than dynamic adjustment. Late Chunking (Günther et al., 2024) applies context-aware embeddings before slicing to retain long-range dependencies; however, it ultimately outputs flat lists that are often insufficient to capture deep physical topologies, such as nested section-item relationships. Inspired by the Mixture of Experts (MoE), MoC (Zhao et al., 2025) and MoG (Zhong et al., 2025) treat various chunking strategies as expert modules managed by query-driven routers; however, their performance remains bounded by the underlying heuristics. While hierarchical retrieval mechanisms like Parent-Child Indexing attempt context augmentation, child chunks often degenerate into “semantic islands” due to a lack of intrinsically independent context. Furthermore, many advanced RAG frameworks rely on heavyweight external graph databases, introducing substantial I/O overhead during preprocessing. Liu et al. (2024) noted that context utilization decays with position, suggesting that simple hierarchical associations are insufficient for high-precision retrieval. Unlike these methods, TopoChunker utilizes a lightweight, inmemory SIR with explicit parent-child-sibling relationships. By dynamically injecting Topological Lineage, it effectively facilitates multi-hop reasoning over previously fragmented knowledge.
2.3 Agentic Workflows and Adaptive
Diagnostics for Document Intelligence The integration of autonomous agents introduces “reasoning-before-action” capabilities to handle unstructured document anomalies. Traditional models based on LSTM or BERT are limited by narrow context windows and single-level processing. RAG-oriented approaches like PIC (Wang et al., 2025) use pseudo-instructions for guidance but exhibit weak spatial awareness, struggling with het-

text:
erogeneous elements like nested tables. Although Vision-Language Models (VLMs) offer superior layout perception, their high computational overhead often limits their viability for large-scale deployment. Furthermore, while emerging agentic chunking frameworks introduce dynamic decision-making, they typically lack rigorous quantitative diagnostics and closed-loop optimization mechanisms. As a result, they tend to apply LLM reasoning uniformly across all text, which incurs excessive token expenditure on standard structural elements. To mitigate these inefficiencies, TopoChunker employs an Inspector Agent designed around a cost-risk minimization objective to prevent redundant processing. Paired with the Refiner Agent’s ReAct-driven diagnostic loop, this "Diagnosis-Execution-Audit" paradigm strategically allocates computationally expensive generative reasoning to high-complexity data points, thereby improving both topological fidelity and inference efficiency compared to existing agentic workflows.
3 Method
3.1 Cognitive Perception and Adaptive
Routing TopoChunker employs a three-stage agentic architecture to address the limitations of linear ETL pipelines. As illustrated in Figure 1, the workflow transitions from perception and topological modeling to metadata assembly. The decision-making of all agents is driven by reasoning-focused LLMs (e.g., DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025)). The process begins in the Cognitive Perception Layer, where the Inspector Agent evaluates the trade-off between potential information loss and computational cost.
3.1.1 Active Probing and Path Selection
The Inspector Agent employs an active probing paradigm. Rather than consuming the entirety of the raw document, the agent is provided solely with a document identifier. Operating within the ReAct framework, it autonomously invokes a suite of lightweight API tools—such as metadata parsers, layout density scanners, and hierarchy analyzers— to perform sparse sampling. Through these targeted queries, the agent incrementally constructs a document-specific topology fingerprint ⃗f. Crucially, this tool-driven decoupling compresses the document’s spatial and hierarchicalcharacteristics into a highly compact token footprint (typically under 200 tokens). By evaluating this lightweight fingerprint instead of the full text, the Inspector avoids optimizing a rigid numeric objective function. Instead, it executes a promptdriven reasoning loop to balance three dimensions: token expenditure, risk of information loss, and structural fidelity. This enables the system to dynamically route heterogeneous inputs through one of three specialized extraction paths at a negligible computational cost: Path 1: Structural Rule. This path is activated for digital documents with clear heading hierarchies when the agent determines that complex visual parsing is computationally redundant. The structural processor performs dynamic hierarchy detection by pre-scanning the document to identify recurring logical patterns (e.g., “Chapter 1,” “Section N,” or nested articles). These patterns are statistically mapped to specific Markdown levels, ensuring the final output explicitly preserves the tree-based skeleton of the original document. Path 2: Semantic Flow. Designed for unstructured narratives where rule-based matching risks high information loss, this path prioritizes semantic continuity. Because these documents lack explicit physical hierarchies, the Inspector directly invokes the LLM-based Semantic_Slicer tool (detailed in Section 3.3) to evaluate the flat text. This decomposes the narrative into preliminary segments based on natural topic transitions. These sequential segments then serve as foundational nodes to construct a localized SIR, maintaining compatibility with downstream metadata assembly and disambiguation phases. Path 3: Visual Topology. For scanned files or documents with complex spatial layouts, the Inspector triggers a vision-centric pipeline. This path leverages layout-aware VLM extractors (e.g., MinerU (Wang et al., 2024)) for physical parsing. Rather than flattening the output into linear text streams, TopoChunker explicitly preserves the extracted coordinates and the physical integrity of non-textual elements (e.g., tables and charts), directly mapping this spatial data into our logical Markdown representation.
3.2 Topological Modeling and SIR
Construction Although the three routing paths employ distinct extraction mechanisms, their outputs are unified

3.3 Semantic Refinement and Context
Assembly The premise of the SIR topology is that text under a specific heading natively forms a coherent semantic unit. However, encoding arbitrarily long structural blocks dilutes their representation in the embedding space, degrading downstream retrieval precision. To reconcile structural completeness with retrieval efficiency, the Refiner Agent manages the text segments via a ReAct paradigm (Yao et al., 2023). To achieve this, it is equipped with three tools: SIR_Query ,Semantic_Slicer , and Chunk_Enhancer. The agent executes the refinement and assembly pipeline through a sequence of operations:

If a node exceeds this limit, the agent invokes the Semantic_Slicer . Internally, this tool uses regular expressions to explicitly identify sentence boundaries and assigns sequential IDs (e.g., [S0],[S 1], . . . ). These indexed sentences are then passed to the LLM via a zero-shot prompt to identify boundary IDs where significant topic or temporal shifts occur. To prevent hallucination errors, the generated IDs are deterministically validated against the valid sequence before execution. This partitions oversized nodes into contextually coherent sub-chunks without disrupting the underlying narrative flow.
3.3.2 Semantic Signature Generation
Once capacity constraints are met, the agent applies theChunk_Enhancer to transform raw segments into self-contained units. To maximize lexical discriminability, the enhancer prompts the LLM to generate a concise, 3-to-8 word thematic title that abstracts the core topic, avoiding the simple extraction of the first sentence. This ensures the chunk is indexed with a precise semantic signature rather than relying solely on generalized macro-headers.
3.3.3 Topological Context Disambiguation
To resolve semantic fragmentation and eliminate “semantic islands,” the agent performs a final context-grounding step at the chunk level. It audits the chunk’s payload for unresolved pronominal anaphora, demonstrative references, and isolated context-dependent terminology (e.g., domain-specific acronyms). Upon detecting these contextual voids, the agent triggers SIR_Query . Instead of executing external graph database queries, SIR_Query deterministically traverses the in-memory object tree. By navigating topological pointers (e.g.,parent,prev_sibling), the agent retrieves entity definitions and macro-context fromancestor nodes. This resolved context is then explicitly fused into the chunk’s text, providing downstream models with a logically complete and structurally grounded premise.
4 Experiments
4.1 Experimental Setup
Datasets.We evaluate our framework on two benchmarks: GutenQA and GovReport. Specifically, GutenQA comprises 100 public domain narrative books serving as the retrieval corpus, paired with 3,000 specific question-answer pairs for evaluation. For GovReport, we constructed a test set by sampling 500 queries, evaluated following the same inference methodology as GutenQA. We compare TopoChunker against four representative paradigms to evaluate its effectiveness. To ensure a fair comparison, all dense retrieval evaluations use BGE-m3 as the underlying embedding model. •Fixed-Size Chunking (FC200): A standard heuristic baseline that splits text into rigid blocks of up to 200 tokens. •Semantic Chunker(Xiao et al., 2024): A dynamic method that determines boundaries based on embedding similarity shifts at the sentence level. •Proposition-Level Chunking(Chen et al., 2024): A granular strategy decomposing text into self-contained atomic factual statements. •LumberChunker(Duarte et al., 2024): A recent approach using LLMs to predict optimal breaks. To align with TopoChunker’s setup, we deploy DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025) as the backbone for both LumberChunker and our framework, uniformly setting the sampling temperature to 0.1 to promote deter-

4.2 Quantitative Evaluation
4.2.1 Retrieval Performance
As shown in Table 1, TopoChunker outperforms all evaluated baselines across both unstructured and highly structured domains, achieving the highest performance in both absolute retrieval (Recall@ k) and ranking quality (DCG@k). Traditional methods exhibit limited robustness to structural variance. On the GovReport benchmark, FC200 and Semantic Chunker achieve lower R@3 scores of 32.25% and 55.37%, respectively, primarily because they mechanically sever logical flow. While Proposition-Level chunking performs moderately better by isolating factual statements, its excessive fragmentation often obscures the broader context necessary for accurate dense matching. Conversely, TopoChunker maintains contextual integrity regardless of document complexity. On the unstructured GutenQA dataset, it outperforms the LLM-guided LumberChunker, achieving an R@3 of64.59%. This indicates that our Semantic Flow routing preserves self-contained contexts even in flat texts. The performance gap widens on the dense hierarchies of GovReport, where TopoChunker achieves an R@3 of83.26%and a D@3 of76.59%. This margin over the strongest baselines demonstrates the effectiveness of our Topological Lineage and Semantic Signature mechanisms. By synthesizing abstract chunk titles and retaining ancestral metadata, TopoChunker mitigates “feature dilution” in the embedding space, enabling precise semantic matching for complex queries.4.2.2 Generation Accuracy We evaluate end-to-end RAG generation using an LLM-as-a-judge pipeline powered by GPT-4. To validate the reliability of this automated metric and mitigate potential biases, we conducted a manual audit. We randomly sampled 100 generated QA pairs across all methods for blind human expert annotation. The human annotations achieved a 92% agreement rate with the GPT-4 judgments, confirming the validity of our evaluation protocol. As Figure 2 illustrates, TopoChunker outperforms all evaluated baselines across both datasets. It achieves 64.0% accuracy on the unstructured GutenQA (+8.0% absolute improvement over the strongest baseline, LumberChunker) and reaches 82.0% on the highly structured GovReport dataset, outperforming heuristic baselines like FC200 by a wide margin. This performance advantage is primarily attributed to the framework’s topological context disambiguation. Baseline chunkers often arbitrarily partition text, creating “semantic islands” with unresolved anaphora (e.g., dangling pronouns like “it” or “the department”) and decoupled terminology. In contrast, TopoChunker addresses these contextual gaps by explicitly injecting inherited parent headers, ancestral entities, and prerequisite definitions into the retrieved segments. Providing the generative LLM with a logically complete and selfcontained premise reduces context drift, thereby minimizing hallucinations and yielding structurally grounded responses.
4.3 Token Efficiency
TopoChunker dynamically scales token cost based on document complexity. Unlike LumberChunker’s constant 1.65× overhead (due to iterative fulltext scanning), TopoChunker decouples physical extraction from semantic reasoning. LLM consumption is strictly limited to the Inspector for routing and the Refiner for auditing, avoiding redundant processing of standard structures. We evaluate token costs on a mixed-complexity corpus (60% simple, 40% complex layouts) using a standard 10,000-token document (Figure 3). For simple documents, TopoChunker consumes 8,500 tokens for routine context disambiguation, requiring fewer tokens than full-text scanning. For complex cases requiring VLM layout parsing, consumption peaks at 18,800 tokens. Despite this premium over LumberChunker

4.4 Module-wise Ablation Study
We conduct an ablation study on the mixedcomplexity corpus to isolate the contributions of theRefiner Agent(semantic quality) and theInspector Agent(routing efficiency).
4.4.1 Impact of the Refiner Agent
As Table 2 shows, extracting raw topology is insufficient for high-quality retrieval. Removing the Refiner (w/o Refiner) leads to a 6.76-point degradation in Recall@3 and an 11.0% decrease in generation accuracy. Without capacity auditing, oversized nodes suffer from vector dilution, and unresolved anaphora create “semantic islands” that introduce ambiguity to the generative LLM.4.4.2 Impact of the Inspector Agent Replacing the dynamic Inspector with static routing pipelines highlights its role in balancing cost and performance. Lightweight static paths (Topo- Static-P1/P2) lower token costs (0.80x and 0.95x) but fail to adequately process complex layouts, decreasing Recall@3 to 77.80% and 79.20%. Conversely, forcing all documents through the VLM pipeline (Topo-Static-P3) yields high accuracy (82.85% Recall@3) but incurs a substantial 1.88x token overhead. The fullTopoChunkerdynamically routes simple documents, achieving the highest overall accuracy (83.26% Recall@3) while maintaining an average token cost of 1.26x. This represents a 32.9% cost reduction over the forced VLM approach and a 23.5% reduction over LumberChunker.
5 Conclusion
In this paper, we introduce TopoChunker, a topology-aware framework for document chunking in RAG pipelines. By mapping heterogeneous documents onto a Structured Intermediate Representation (SIR) via a dual-agent architecture— comprising an Inspector Agent for adaptive routing and a Refiner Agent for semantic auditing— our approach mitigates “semantic islands” and resolves anaphoric conflicts. Evaluations on unstructured narratives (GutenQA) and highly structured reports (GovReport) demonstrate that TopoChunker achieves state-of-the-art retrieval and generation accuracy. These results indicate that preserving and explicitly injecting topological metadata is critical for robust RAG systems. Limitations While TopoChunker improves retrieval quality and structural fidelity, the current framework has two primary limitations: Upstream Parsing Dependency:For documents with complex visual layouts routed through Path 3, the system relies on external VLM extractors (e.g., MinerU) for physical parsing. Consequently, upstream OCR inaccuracies or layout misclassifications can cascade, propagating errors to the downstream Structured Intermediate Representation (SIR). Inference Latency:Although our routing mechanism reduces overall token expenditure, the agentic paradigm inherently introduces higher inference

latency compared to deterministic heuristic chunkers. The reliance on instruction-tuned LLMs for dynamic routing and semantic auditing requires sequential API calls. This latency overhead poses challenges for real-time or latency-sensitive RAG applications. Ethics Statement In this work, we conduct a manual human evaluation to validate the reliability of our automated LLM-as-a-judge pipeline. We are committed to adhering to the ACL Ethics Policy and address the relevant ethical considerations below: Human Labor and Participation:The human evaluation involved annotating 100 randomly sampled generated QA pairs to assess generation accuracy. This process was conducted entirely by the authors of this paper. As the evaluation was performed by the research team as part of their academic duties, no external annotators or crowdsourcing platforms were used, and no additional financial compensation was applicable. Anonymity and Bias Control:To ensure the objectivity of the evaluation, the generated outputs were shuffled and anonymized so that the authors were unaware of which specific method (baseline vs. TopoChunker) produced each response during the annotation process. No personally identifiable information (PII) was involved in the evaluation. Data Risks and Content Considerations:The datasets utilized in this study, GutenQA and Gov- Report, are publicly available benchmarks consisting of public domain literature and government documents. We have screened the sampled data and confirmed that they do not contain sensitive personal information, toxic language, or offensive content that could pose ethical risks.

(1)Level 1 (Top Secret): Refers to data that, if leaked, would directly lead to the loss of the Company’s core competitiveness or seriously threaten national security. The scope is strictly limited to: Core Technology: Proprietary large model training weights (Checkpoints), unpatented chip architecture diagrams, and hardware security module (HSM) Root Keys. (2)Level 2 (Confidential): Refers to data that, if leaked, could cause significant damage to the Company’s reputation or finances. The scope includes: User Privacy: Real-name user databases containing ID numbers, facial recognition features, and bank card numbers. Business Secrets: Key Account (KA) lists in CRM systems, exclusive supply chain pricing agreements, and quarterly detailed financial statements (unpublished). Source Code: Application-layer code for non-core business systems and API interface documentation. (3)Level 3 (Internal Use): Refers to data known only to internal employees, including administrative notices, desensitized weekly operational reports, internal directories, and general technical documentation. Article 2 [Access Control Strategies for Each Level]Unauthorized access to sensitive data is strictly prohibited. The circulation and access of data at all levels must comply with the following mandatory regulations: (1) For Level 1 Data: Implement a "Zero Trust" access strategy. It must be viewed via intranet terminals within a physically isolated Clean Room. Any form of downloading, exporting, or transmission via the Internet is strictly prohibited. Access requires dual approval (Double-Check) from the CTO and the Compliance Director. (2) For Level 2 Data: Export is strictly prohibited in principle. If export is necessary, it must be approved by a department head at L8 level or above, and the system must forcibly add an invisible Digital Watermark containing the employee ID and timestamp. (3) For Level 3 Data: Access and circulation are permitted on Company intranet office terminals, but uploading to unauthorized public cloud storage platforms is prohibited. (4) For Level 4 Data (Public/Desensitized): Implement a "Pre-release Review" system. Although such data is permitted for external disclosure (e.g., financial report summaries, marketing materials), it must undergo content compliance review by PR or Legal departments before release. (5) For Audit and Monitoring: Implement full-link "Behavioral Profiling" monitoring. All cross-level data access behaviors must retain immutable Audit Logs for a retention period of no less than 12 months. The system must deploy UEBA policies to trigger real-time blocking. Chapter 2: Organizational Guarantee and Legal Liability Article 1 [Organizational Structure and Responsibilities]The Company establishes the Data Security Committee (DSC) as the highest decision-making body, with the CEO serving as the group leader. Heads of business lines (BP) are the primary persons responsible for data security in their respective departments and must sign the "Annual Data Security Responsibility Letter." Article 2 [Data Security Emergency Response]In the event of security incidents such as data leakage, tampering, or loss, the discoverer shall report to the Security Operations Center (SOC) within 15 minutes. For major leakage incidents involving Level 1 or Level 2 data, the SOC must activate the Level 1 Emergency Plan within 1 hour. Article 3 [Personnel Training and Assessment]The HR Department, in conjunction with the Information Security Department, shall organize company-wide data security awareness training quarterly. Personnel in core positions involving contact with Level 1 or Level 2 data must pass the "Data Security Compliance Exam" annually.

C Agent System Prompts
[TABLE: presents the core system prompts utilized by the dual-agent architecture. The Inspector Agent]
executes the multi-criteria reasoning loop for adaptive routing, while the Refiner Agent enforces strict verbatim preservation during semantic auditing and contextual disambiguation.
[TABLE: System Prompts for the Inspector and Refiner Agents.]
Part I: Inspector Agent Agent Role:Strategic Cognitive Planner for document routing. Core Task:You will be provided solely with a Document ID. You must autonomously invoke analytical tools to extract the document’s structural fingerprint ( ⃗f) and determine the optimal routing pathway by heuristically balancing three dimensions: computational cost (token expenditure), risk of information loss, and structural fidelity. Step 1 (Active Probing via Tools):Using the provided Document ID, invoke the available lightweight API tools (e.g., analyze_metadata,probe_layout_complexity,test_rule_adherence) to perform sparse sampling. Do not attempt to process the raw document text. Rely strictly on the JSON responses from these tools to assess visual element density, scanned status, and textual hierarchy clarity. Step 2 (Multi-Criteria Reasoning & Routing):Evaluate the tool outputs to balance the trade-offs and select one routing path: •Select VISUAL_TOPOLOGY (Path 3) for scanned or visually complex documents to prevent structural loss despite higher computational cost. • SelectSTRUCTURAL_RULE(Path 1) for digital documents with clear heading hierarchies to minimize cost. • SelectSEMANTIC_FLOW(Path 2) for unstructured narratives to prioritize semantic continuity. Output Format:Output the final decision strictly as a JSON object: { "selected_path": "VISUAL_TOPOLOGY" | "STRUCTURAL_RULE" | "SEMANTIC_FLOW", "confidence_score": float, "risk_score": float, "reason": "string (concise justification based on tool observations)" } Part II: Refiner Agent Agent Role:Expert Document Contextualization Agent. Core Task:Execute semantic auditing and topological context disambiguation to transform raw document sections into self-contained Semantic Atoms optimized for RAG. Core Principle:Preserve the original text verbatim. You must not rewrite or paraphrase the text body. Your value is added strictly through Metadata Headers and Contextual Disambiguation. Strategy 1 (Title Generation):Create a concise (3-8 words) title capturing the main topic. Do not recycle the first sentence. Maximize lexical discriminability. Strategy 2 (Contextual Disambiguation):Scan for unresolved pronouns or isolated references. If the referent exists within the chunk, do nothing. If missing, invoke the SIR_Query tool to retrieve ancestor nodes. If the definitive entity is found, create a "Context Supplement" field. Capacity Auditing & Operational Rules:If the system flags the current node as oversized ( is_oversized = True ), you must invoke the Semantic_Slicer tool first to explicitly identify optimal sentence boundaries, and then process each resulting segment independently. Do not merge them back. Output Format:Wrap results in<final_chunks>tags as a JSON list of strings. Each string must follow this template: [ "# {Semantic Signature} Context Supplement: {Entity Mappings} // Omit if unnecessary {Original Text Content Verbatim}" ]
